questions.question: Isolate in the lab that is a GNB. On TSI, there is an alkaline slant with scant production of H2S. It is citrate negative, lysine positive and urease negative.

parts.text: 3 antigens that you would test and briefly describe each.

questions.model_answer: This biochemical profile (alkaline slant/acid butt with scant H2S, citrate-negative, lysine-positive, urease-negative) is classic for Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi. 3 antigens to test: (1) O antigen (somatic lipopolysaccharide antigen) - defines the serogroup; (2) H antigen (flagellar protein antigen) - defines the serotype, and can undergo phase variation between phase 1 and phase 2 flagellar forms; (3) Vi antigen (capsular polysaccharide virulence antigen) - present on S. Typhi (and some S. Paratyphi C), associated with virulence/immune evasion and used in Vi-conjugate typhoid vaccines.
questions.beyond_mandell: Standard clinical microbiology serotyping scheme (Kauffmann-White scheme) for Salmonella.

parts.text: a) What are 3 immune mediated complications of infection?
b) What are 2 treatment options? When should they be considered?

cohort_answer.text:
HUS; Reactive arthritis; Encephalopathy (Ekiri syndrome - more in pediatrics, after S. sonnei or S. flexneri)
Macrolides or Fluoroquinolones (or ceftriaxone if from area with high resistance like Asia), based on in vitro susceptibility. All infections should be treated. Macrolide or FQ: 3 days; SXT or CTRX: 5 days

questions.question: According to CLSI 2016, which 3 antibiotics should be tested and reported for Salmonella and Shigella isolated from stool? Report only for fecal typhoidal salmonella (typhi and paratyphi), and shigella.

cohort_answer.text: Ampicillin, Fluoroquinolones, Septra (if extraintestinal, also report 3rd gen cephalosporins; azithro has breakpoints now but not reported)

questions.question: PM 7. Your organization uses MALDI-TOF for identification of bacteria. Girl presents with bloody diarrhea and reports Shigella flexneri

parts.text: Why should MALDI-TOF NOT be used for identification of this organism? (1)
Explain the concept of "mass spec" and how it allows identification. (2)

cohort_answer.text: Shigella too similar to E. coli (metabolically-challenged E. coli, same ribosomal proteins) - MALDI not reliable. Mass spec: colony placed on matrix, laser causes desorption/ionization of rRNA macroprotein; fragments ionized and accelerated in electromagnetic field, hit detector based on mass:charge ratio (bigger proteins = slower flight, time of flight TOF); spectra unique fingerprint compared to standardized database. Advantages: rapid identification, limited need for lab personnel, highly accurate, less subjective than biochemicals. Disadvantages: organism needs to be in database, does not give susceptibility patterns, expensive machine, unable to identify very closely related organisms (e.g. Strep mitis/oralis, E. coli/Shigella).

questions.question: Shigella dysenteriae.
questions.model_answer:
a) 3 immune-mediated complications: (1) hemolytic uremic syndrome (from Shiga toxin-mediated endothelial injury, most classically associated with S. dysenteriae type 1); (2) reactive arthritis (post-infectious, HLA-B27 associated); (3) Guillain-Barre syndrome (rare, post-infectious).
b) 2 empiric treatment options: ciprofloxacin and azithromycin (ceftriaxone is an acceptable alternative).

questions.question:
Q41 (2013 AM)
Stool pathogens, various microbiological features, match pathogen to features. Micro features given: Microaerophilic grows on charcoal; H2S producing NLF, catalase negative (maybe oxidase negative) curved GNB; NLF catalase negative (may be oxidase negative). Organisms: Vibrio, Shigella sonnei, Salmonella typhimurium, Campylobacter, Aeromonas

cohort_answer.text: Microaerophilic grows on charcoal - Campylobacter. H2S producing NLF, catalase negative (maybe oxidase negative) curved GNB - Salmonella. NLF catalase negative (may be oxidase negative) - Shigella. Additional detail: Vibrio - gram negative, non-lactose fermenter, curved-rod (comma) shape, facultative anaerobe, oxidase positive, motile with polar flagella. Shigella sonnei - nonmotile, facultatively anaerobic GNR, non-lactose fermenter, no H2S, indole positive, ferments glucose/urea, oxidase negative, differentiated by ornithine decarboxylase expression. Salmonella typhimurium - gram negative facultatively anaerobic Enterobacteriaceae, non-lactose fermenter, oxidase negative, produces H2S. Campylobacter - spiral shape, long flagella, mostly microaerophilic, thermophilic, nonfermentative, oxidase and catalase positive, urease negative (vs Helicobacter urease positive). Aeromonas - gram negative, non-lactose fermenter, oxidase positive, ferments glucose

Reactive arthritis, conjunctivitis, urethritis (post-infectious arthritis in ~2% of S. flexneri infections, requires genetic predisposition); Ekiri syndrome (lethal toxic encephalopathy); Erythema nodosum; GN; Guillain Barre syndrome; HUS/TTP (associated with Shiga toxin-producing Shigella, most often S. dysenteriae) (speaker notes: Ekiri syndrome, erythema nodosum, GBS)
Ceftriaxone; FQ (Cipro is treatment of choice); Azithromycin (if susceptible). Duration: 5 days for beta lactam, 3 days for azithro/FQ; immunocompromised treat 7-10 days
